name: Wheatstone bridge
description: The classic way to measure a small change of resistance, here a field sensor. Magnetoresistance's two strips share a supply of 12 at their right ends: the long one, whose resistance barely changes in a field, and the short wide one, whose resistance grows with the field's strength. Each strip's left end goes to ground through a resistor, 5 for the long strip and 1.5 for the short one, and a voltmeter reads the difference between those two ends. It reads zero, the bridge balanced, when the strips' resistances stand in the resistors' ratio: the short one 1.5/5 of the long one. Set your solenoid so that the voltmeter reads between -0.3 and 0.3 (averaged over $t = 10$ to $150$). Real sensors work this way: magnetoresistors in a bridge, its small output read by an amplifier.

reality.represents: A Wheatstone bridge reading a magnetoresistor: a field sensor

remarks.line: A bridge balances on a ratio
remarks.detail: It reads zero when its arms' resistances stand in the same ratio, so a small change shows as a voltage from zero: how strain gauges and field sensors are read.
The short wide strip's contacts short out its Hall field, its carriers' paths bend, and it resists more in either field direction: InSb field plates in sensor bridges.

remarks.line: Two strips and two ideal resistors
remarks.detail: A full sensor bridge has four matched elements whose drifts cancel; here two arms are ideal lumped resistors, so the long strip's own small magnetoresistance shifts the balance a little.

remarks.line: A classical metal, a semiconductor by its ratios
remarks.detail: The carriers are classical particles at the lattice's temperature bouncing off fixed ion cores (the Drude model). A real metal's electrons are a degenerate quantum gas whose own ratios (plasma oscillations per collision, screening per free path) the model cannot afford; its carriers have a lightly doped semiconductor's ratios (the Scales section names which), which conducts by the same laws.

The strip is infinitely long along z, its carriers lines of charge moving as one: currents are per unit length, and the noise is larger than a real conductor's, whose carriers move independently along its length.
Supplies, resistors, capacitors and coils are ideal lumped parts, per unit length of the tube; they drive the electrodes and feel the current the electrons induce (Ramo).

electrodes.label: long strip, left end (to ground through 5; the voltmeter's +)
wide strip, left contact (to ground through 1.5; the voltmeter's −)
